subject: Business Models
title: Tiered Pricing
description: A short lesson to help you apply Tiered Pricing.

hook.text: Basic, Pro, Enterprise. Every SaaS product offers three plans. It's not random—it's psychology.

buildup.text: Three tiers exploit 'anchoring.' The expensive plan makes the middle one look like a bargain.

discovery.text: Most customers pick the middle tier. Companies design it to be the most profitable option.

twist.text: The cheapest tier often exists just to make the middle one attractive. It's a decoy, not a product.

climax.text: Tiered pricing captures different willingness to pay from different segments with one product.

punchline.text: Three tiers, one goal: make you pick the middle one.

quiz.question: What psychological effect do three pricing tiers exploit?

details.summary: Tiered pricing offers multiple product bundles at different price points, each targeting a distinct customer segment. A free tier attracts users, a mid-tier serves growing teams, and an enterprise tier captures large organizations willing to pay premium prices for advanced features.
details.whyItMatters: Tiered pricing maximizes revenue by capturing willingness to pay across different customer segments while maintaining a single product. Proper tier design is one of the highest-leverage activities in SaaS pricing strategy.
takeaways: Multiple price points capture value from different customer segments
Feature differentiation between tiers drives upgrade motivation
Three to four tiers typically optimize revenue across the customer base

faq.question: How should features be allocated across pricing tiers?
faq.answer: Core features that define the product belong in every tier. Features that scale with team size should differentiate mid-tier from basic. Enterprise features address security, compliance, and administrative control needs. Each tier should feel complete while creating clear upgrade motivation.

faq.question: How many pricing tiers should a product offer?
faq.answer: Three to four tiers is the standard. Fewer tiers leave money on the table by not segmenting willingness to pay. More than four creates decision paralysis. Research shows that most buyers choose the middle option, so the middle tier should be the most profitable.
